## §CORE-05. A PAGED READ IS A READ OF THE DATA — one stable key, every row exactly once (owner report 2026-10-14)

Owner, 2026-10-14, verbatim: *"do tehy mean there is only ne accoutn for 27 lines"* — about a row of
the Store Takeover Evaluation's multi-line account report claiming **27 activated lines** on one
subscriber account in June 2026, the same five IMEIs printed three times over.

**That account carries nine lines.** The report was not wrong about the account; the read underneath it
was wrong about the feed.

### CORE-05.1 THE CLASS, not the instance

> **`OFFSET` / `range()` paging without an `ORDER BY` pages an UNORDERED set, so the backend may serve
> one row in two pages and never serve another at all.**

Postgres promises nothing about row order without `ORDER BY`, and it does not have to — each page is a
fresh plan over a table other sessions are writing. `core/feed_read.read_all`, the one home for "give
me ALL of this feed" (§19.48), asked for rows 0–999, then 1000–1999, and so on, with no order at all.

**MEASURED LIVE 2026-10-14** (read-only, Supabase REST, `commcalc.prospect_feed_row`, one prospect
holding 137,374 rows, the two reads run back to back):

| read | rows returned | distinct | duplicate copies | never served |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no `ORDER BY` — what the one home did | 137,374 | **88,294** | **49,080** | **49,080** |
| `order=id.asc` | 137,374 | 137,374 | 0 | 0 |

So **a third of that feed was invisible** to every surface reading it while another third was counted
twice — and nothing reported a problem. The loop still ended on a short page and still returned a
plausible row count, which is the §19.48 failure mode again (*a read that is wrong quietly*) and worse
than a literal ceiling: a ceiling at least drops the same rows every time, so the figure is at least
stable enough to notice.

On the owner's three pasted rows the true figures are **9, 7 and 8 lines**, against 27, 26 and 26 on
screen. The duplicated rows also flipped two derived answers: `add_a_lines` read 4 where the account
has 1, and `same_processor_account` read "yes" for an account whose lines were rung at more than one
store. A duplicate row is not a cosmetic inflation — it changes every count, share and yes/no derived
from the set.

### CORE-05.2 THE FIX — in the one home, and it cannot un-wire

`feed_read.ORDER_KEY` (`"id"`) is applied on **every page**, and it is **appended**, so a caller that
orders by its own column keeps that order and gets a *total* one — verified against the installed
postgrest builder, whose `order()` concatenates onto any existing order rather than replacing it.
Every table read through this module carries `id` (verified live 2026-10-14: `raw_mi`, `raw_sales`,
`raw_comp_report`, `raw_payment_detail`, `store_expenses`, `payment_categories`, `asset_ledger`,
`prospect_feed_row`, `carrier_category_map`, `account_statements`). A table whose stable key is spelled
otherwise passes `order=`; a read that **cannot** be ordered RAISES `IncompleteRead` rather than
returning a scrambled feed, because a scrambled feed is indistinguishable from a correct one
downstream — exactly the property that let this run for months.

### CORE-05.3 THE SIBLING — the appeal-recovery engine's own copy of the loop

`recovery/engine._read_all` kept a private page loop, and its own docstring already named the hazard it
then walked into: a `.limit(N)` shot dropped rows *"with no ORDER BY, so WHICH rows vanished was
arbitrary from one call to the next"* — and the loop that replaced the limit paged without an ORDER BY
either. It builds the `pay_by_imei` / `mi_by_serial` evidence dictionaries, so **a device whose payment
row was never served reads as "no evidence found"**, which is precisely the input that buckets an
appeal as `not_recoverable`. Missing evidence and absent evidence are indistinguishable downstream, so
the engine could not detect its own blind spot. It dereferences the one home now and keeps no loop.

### CORE-05.4 THE 99 THAT ARE STILL WRONG, counted rather than assumed away

This is the honest part. `read_all` has 30 call sites; the rest of the backend pages in **private
copies of the same loop**, and an AST scan of `backend/app` counts **99 `range()` reads with no
`.order()` on their chain**, across 32 files. Among them are paths that move money:
`account/coa._fetch_all` (the P&L's own table reader), `account/residual_subs` (4),
`account/statement_engine` (2), `account/ledger_pnl`, `account/ma_store_pnl.load_store_index`,
`account/device_cogs`, `commcalc/commission_engine` (2), `commcalc/payout_accrual` (7),
`commcalc/ma_recon`, `commcalc/whatif` (7).

`harness_feed_read_lock.py` §C pins that number and requires EQUALITY: a new unordered paged read fails
the build, and converting one to the one home requires lowering the pin in the same commit. So the
count on screen is always the real state of the platform rather than a claim that the platform is
fixed. Converting them is the follow-up work, one subsystem per PR, because each is a money path and a
blind conversion of a money path is how a quiet read becomes a quiet booking.

### CORE-05.5 PROOF

`harness_feed_read_lock.py` — **19 passed / 0 failed**, DB-free. The one home is driven over a fake
backend that models PostgREST: ordered, it serves a sorted slice; unordered, a differently permuted one
per page — the live failure, deterministically. **§A2 is armed**: replayed against the pre-fix loop the
same fixture returns 2,500 rows holding only 2,426 distinct, 74 duplicate copies and 74 rows never
served, so the check fails on the old code and the detector is not decorative. §A5 proves a caller's
own order survives, §A6 that an orderless read is refused rather than served, §A7 that a failed page
raises and names the key, §B that the module keeps one `.range(` behind an `.order(` and still carries
no row ceiling, §C the sibling ratchet with four negative controls, §D that the recovery engine's loop
is gone and its three evidence reads are still org-scoped.

Same class: §19.48 (a read with a literal ceiling), §19.18 (a mechanism written and its callers left
unwired), §19.46 (a row's month is a property of the row), §COMMCALC-03.9 (an upload that reported
success and answered nothing).

## §CORE-06. A TILE IS A MENU ENTRY, SO IT ANSWERS THE MENU'S QUESTION (owner report 2026-10-14)

Owner: *"I cannot see the schedule on thr app , where are we at making that live to all employees"*.

### CORE-06.1 Two separate facts, and only one of them was a defect

The schedule GATE shipped and merged on 2026-10-05 (§14w PR #389, §14x PR #390, migration **1058**
applied): a rep reads their own shifts, a manager theirs plus whoever works under them, an admin
everything. Verified still live 2026-10-14 — `storeops.app_config.rbac_enabled = true`, all 30 role
rows carry `people_visibility`, 254 shifts stored for the current week across three tenants, and all
73 active rep logins carry an `employee_id` (without one `schedule_emp_ids` returns `set()`, which is
deny-all).

So nothing about the gate was broken. Two other things were:

- **CONFIG, not code.** `/storeops/schedule` is `tileOnly` (Phase W2.1, the "cleaner look"
  directive), so the sidebar never lists it — the Workforce hub tile is its only door. And the
  Luxelink `sales_rep` role carries `permissions.modules.storeops = false`, which closes that door
  for **39 of the 111 active logins**. One checkbox on Admin → Roles & Access, no migration.
- **CODE.** The door itself never asked whether the person looking at it could walk through.

### CORE-06.2 THE CLASS, not the instance

Five surfaces render `HubTiles`, and each answered *"which of these pages may this viewer open"* for
itself — three copies of one predicate stack, and two surfaces with no answer at all:

| surface | the viewer gate |
|---|---|
| `(platform)/hub/[group]/page.tsx` | the stack, inline |
| `(platform)/compliance/page.tsx` | the same stack, **retyped** |
| `(platform)/admin/dashboards/page.tsx` | a third copy — a **different** question (what a DESIGNER may place) |
| `(platform)/storeops/page.tsx` | hand-woven `HubGroup[]` literal, **none** |
| `(platform)/payroll/page.tsx` | hand-woven `HubGroup[]` literal, **none** |

Measured against the live NAV and the live role rows, the Workforce hub showed a store-scoped rep
**11 of its 21 interior links** and **2 of its 6 KPI tiles** pointing at pages `canAccessPath`
bounces: `/storeops/timeclock`, `/attendance`, `/accountability`, `/employees`, `/reports`,
`/visits`, `/visits/settings`, `/visits/plan`, `/reviews/config`, `/setup/stores`,
`/setup/employees`. That is the **"the tab is there but clicking it does nothing"** failure
`rbac.ts` already names twice (TKT-1009, TKT-1012) — reached through a tile instead of the menu,
because the two curated hubs were the consumers that never asked. A tile is a menu entry; it owes
the menu's answer.

### CORE-06.3 THE FIX — one home, dereferenced, and it cannot un-wire

**`frontend/src/lib/hub-gate.ts::useHubGate()`** is the ONE home for "may this viewer open this page
from a tile". It mirrors the sidebar's own chain verbatim (`(platform)/layout.tsx`): RBAC only while
login is enforced **and** a session exists (the open app shows everything, as the sidebar's `open`
path does), then `platformOK`, the tenant capability flag, the active-carrier lens, the tenant
vertical, and the tenant nav-layout `hidden` override.

- `groupOK(group)` — the GROUP half of the same §38 question: a platform-only nav group opens for the
  platform super admin alone. It lives here too because `/compliance` resolved its own group with no
  group gate at all, and only the item half was ever applied there.
- `gateItems(items)` — for a hub built from NAV items (the generic hub, `/compliance`).
- `canOpen(href)` — for a hand-woven tile or KPI literal, whose entries are hrefs, not NAV items.
- `gateHubGroups(groups)` — `canOpen` over a `HubGroup[]` literal, dropping a tile left with no
  reachable page (exactly as `tile-hubs.ts::layoutToHubGroups` already drops one).

**Why `canOpen` falls back to `canAccessPath`.** A hand-woven tile may name an href with no NAV entry
of its own. Fail-closed would hide a page the route guard would admit — a tile vanishing for no
reason is the same defect wearing a hat. So an href NAV does not carry is answered by `canAccessPath`,
which IS the route guard, and the two can never disagree.

**`/admin/dashboards` is excused on purpose**, and the harness pins the excuse: it answers the
designer's question, not the viewer's, and its renderer re-applies the viewer gate. The rule §23g
already states — *widening what a DESIGNER may place must never widen what a VIEWER may see* — now
has one implementation instead of three.

Both curated hubs also say so plainly when nothing is reachable, rather than rendering an empty page.

**Three neighbouring locks pinned the gate at its OLD address and went red on the move** — which is
the mechanism working, not a surprise: `harness_hub_cross_module_tiles.py` (§C, 20), `harness_tenant_vertical.py`
(the `verticalOK` wire, 83) and `harness_super_admin_toolbox.py` (§38's E1/E2/G7). Each is repointed at
the one home and each now pins something *wider* than before: the vertical and platform filters are
pinned IN the gate, and all FOUR hubs — not the two that happened to carry a copy — are pinned to
dereference it, with controls proving an un-wired hub goes red.

### CORE-06.4 PROOF

- `frontend/scratchpad/prove_hub_gate.mjs` (38) — verbatim re-impl of `moduleGranted` / `canSeeItem`
  / `canAccessPath` / `canOpen`, run against the **real** NAV parsed out of `rbac.ts`, the **real**
  tile literals parsed out of both curated hubs, and the **real** production role rows. §1 reproduces
  the defect on the pre-fix surface (11 of 21 and 2 of 6) so the regression cannot stop being
  reproduced; §2 asserts nothing offered bounces and nothing legitimate was lost (an admin keeps
  21/21, a store-scoped rep keeps the 10 that are genuinely theirs, Schedule among them); §3 pins
  that ticking Workforce on the one Luxelink role opens Schedule **without** bringing a manager-only
  page with it, plus the deep-link and fallback rules.
- `backend/harness_hub_viewer_gate.py` (53) — the build lock. **Static on purpose**: the failure mode
  is an ABSENT filter, so the page compiles, renders and simply offers links that bounce; no type
  checker and no test of the gate itself can see a caller that never calls it. §A the one home carries
  the whole stack, §B every `HubTiles` consumer dereferences it, §C nobody retypes it, §D the curated
  KPI rows are gated too, §E eight negative controls proving each check bites.


## §CORE-07. A LOGIN IS NOBODY UNTIL IT IS LINKED TO ITS PERSON (owner report 2026-10-14)

Owner: *"all stores should be able to see their dashboard with commissions earned and their schedules
and submit their closing at night with their app, then send me the process to add app access to all of
them"*. Writing that process meant reading the three paths that create a login. They did not agree.

### CORE-07.1 THE ONE COLUMN, and what NULL costs

A login is tied to its person by `storeops.app_users.employee_id`. With that column NULL the login is
**nobody**, in two places that matter to exactly the request above:

| surface | what a NULL link does | where |
|---|---|---|
| Schedule | `visible_people_keyset` resolves a people_visibility-'self' role to `set(self_employee_ids(app_user))`, which is EMPTY — the rep opens Schedule and sees a blank week | `app/core/scope.py` (§14w) |
| Submit Closing | the submit is refused `closer_no_name` — the caller's own names are read from the employee record this column points at | `closing/router.py::_closer_gate` (§29.7) |

`scope.py`'s own docstring already said it — *"a login with no employee_id on it is nobody and is
shown nothing"* — so the fact was declared. What was missing was every writer honouring it.

### CORE-07.2 THE CLASS, not the instance

Three paths write an `app_users` row for a person, and each decided the link for itself:

| path | sends `employee_id`? | result |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /users/assign` from the Roles **grid** (a row of the employee list) | yes | linked |
| `POST /users/assign` from the **add-a-person form** | no | **NULL** |
| `POST /users/bulk-assign` — the **spreadsheet upload** | no | **NULL** |

So whether a newly provisioned rep could see their own schedule depended on which button the
administrator pressed. Measured live 2026-10-14: the one Vzone `sales_rep` login carries no
`employee_id` and is exactly this instance; Cellfonz's 34 and Luxelink's 39 are all linked only
because they were provisioned from the grid. The spreadsheet path is the one the owner was about to
use for ~23 new logins across NY LOGISTICS, Vzone and the ten un-emailed Cellfonz employees, which is
why it was fixed in the same breath as answering him.

This is the sibling of **§19.45** ("THE ONE MINT" — every `employees` insert passes
`_ensure_employee_id`). That fix gave the *person* a business id; this one makes the *login* point at
it. One without the other is the patchwork CLAUDE.md forbids.

### CORE-07.3 THE FIX — one home, dereferenced, resolved before the write

`app/modules/core/app_user_identity.py::link_employee_id` is the ONE home for the precedence, and it
is **pure** (no client, no I/O, no imports — pinned):

| # | source | why it is in this position |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `request_id` | what the caller explicitly asked for (the grid, or a spreadsheet column) — an administrator naming the person outranks anything inferred |
| 2 | `stored_id` | the link the row already carries; an upsert must never DROP it, or a re-assign that only changes a role blanks that person's schedule |
| 3 | `roster_id` | the employee this email resolves to on **this org's** roster |

`None` (never `""`) when all three are empty, so the column stays NULL rather than holding a falsy
string `self_employee_ids` would read as a real id.

The roster's answer comes from `_ensure_employee`, which was **extended rather than siblinged**: it is
already the one helper both write paths call to put the person on the roster, so it now returns
`(created, employee_id)` and resolves an ALREADY-rostered person too (through
`_employee_id_for_email`, org-scoped, minting via the one mint — never inventing an id). Both handlers
call it **before** writing the login row; resolving after the write leaves the column NULL, and
§E3b of the lock proves that ordering bites.

**The two `app_users` writers that are not people are excused on purpose**, and the lock pins the
excuse: `_provision_tenant` and `create_super_admin` both mint an `'all'`-scope administrator, who is
on no store's roster and whose `people_visibility` short-circuits before the column is read. (The
owner's own super-admin login carries no `employee_id` for that reason, harmlessly.) A **fifth**
insert site fails the build until somebody rules on it — §D1.

### CORE-07.4 PROOF

`backend/harness_app_user_employee_link.py` — **42 passed / 0 failed**, and **armed**: on pristine
`origin/main` it reports **11 failed**, so it is a lock and not a description.

- §A reproduces the consequence against `core/scope.py` **as shipped** (the client is passed as
  `None` on purpose: the 'self' branch returns before any read, so the proof is DB-free and would
  raise rather than quietly pass if that ever changed). A linked rep → `{'E229'}`; an unlinked rep →
  `set()`, which is deny-all and not `None`.
- §B the precedence table, pure. §C the wiring: the helper answers the link on every path, the email
  resolver is org-scoped and mints through the one mint, and neither handler spells an `or` chain of
  its own. §D the excused writers, named. §E nine negative controls, including both pre-fix row
  literals transcribed from `main`.

Not a migration: the column already exists and already has the right meaning. **Rows written before
this ship are not retro-linked** — the one live instance (the Vzone rep) is repaired by re-assigning
that person from the Roles grid, which is config, not a data fix.


## §CORE-08. WHICH PERSON IS THIS NAME (owner report 2026-10-14)

Owner, on the Closing & Cash Pickup Status report (§48.8) he had just been given: *"why does it show
2 reps who worked at the store, it should only show teh actual person who worked for all reporting
not the one with the homw store"*.

Two different defects, both in the same cell, and he named both.

### CORE-08.1 THE INSTANCE, measured on live production

B-1750 on 2026-10-10 had **one man** in it. The report said `Simarjyot Singh, Singh, Simarjyot`.

| signal | table | what it holds for that store-day |
|---|---|---|
| the punch | `storeops.timelog` | `Simarjyot Singh`, 11.77h, store_code `B-1750` |
| the sale | the B2B sales feed | `salesperson = "Singh, Simarjyot"`, `user_login` `Simarjyot`, store `1750 5th Ave` |

`closing/router._who_worked_by_store` unioned those two **name strings**. A union of strings has no
notion of a person, so one man counted twice. Same shape on 2026-10-11.

**The "home store" half is the SECOND defect, and it is not a home store.** `storeops.timelog.store_code`
is where the punch happened, proven rather than assumed: **75 of 89** house employees have punches at
more than one store since 1 July 2026 (`Angie Ramos` → B-1750, B-2509, B-6011). What the owner was
actually seeing is the **scheduled-roster fallback** — when nobody clocked in or rang a sale, the
who-worked signal returned the names the schedule *expected*, tagged `"scheduled"`, inside the same
list as the people who really worked. Every caller had to render that tag or lose it, and the §48.8
report's "Who worked" column did not render it. A guess read as a fact.

### CORE-08.2 THE CLASS, not the instance

**A name string is not an identity.** Every surface that joins two systems' people asks the same
question, and this repo answered it in **nine** places — two of which each declared themselves the
one home for it, for different callers:

| where | the rule it ran | read by |
|---|---|---|
| `commcalc/commission_engine._canon_person` | casefold + single-comma reorder | ~30 commcalc sites; a payout's match key |
| `commcalc/management_incentive._canon_person` | a NEAR-copy that said it mirrored the engine and did not — it reordered ANY number of commas | manager-plan scope match |
| `commcalc/targets_engine.name_key` | uppercase, punctuation out, tokens SORTED | the schedule↔POS target join (§COMMCALC-02) |
| `commcalc/commission_drilldown._tok` | lowercase word-set | the "did you mean" ranking |
| `closing/router._name_match` | equal / contained / shared first token | did this person submit, is this person on the roster |
| `closing/ops_chargebacks._name_match` | a BYTE copy of the above, kept local to dodge an import cycle | the missed-closing sweep |
| `storeops/payroll_identity.person_key` | accent-folded, order-free sorted tokens — **the strongest rule in the building** | the clock feed's employee matcher |
| `storeops/payroll_identity.name_tokens` / `_fold_person` | its two halves | ditto |
| `closing/router._who_worked_by_store` | **no rule at all** — a raw string union | the surface the owner reported |

The last line is the finding. `closing` could not read `storeops/payroll_identity` without a module
cycle and could not read `commission_engine` without importing the commission engine, so the signal
the owner looks at grew the weakest answer in the codebase: none.

### CORE-08.3 THE FIX — one home, four NAMED questions, dereferenced

`backend/app/modules/core/person_identity.py` is the one home. It is **pure at import time** (`re`
only; the accent fold's import is deferred to call time), so every module above can read it and none
can cycle on it. Four questions, named apart so they cannot be mistaken for one another:

| function | forgives | for |
|---|---|---|
| `person_key` | one comma's word order, case, spacing | what ~30 commcalc **money** sites already key on — deliberately **not widened**, because widening a payout join moves money |
| `token_key` | all of the above **and** bare word order | the 2026-09-02 schedule↔POS target join (`KELLIE MARK` vs `Kellie, Mark`) |
| `folded_token_key` | all of the above **and accents** | **the key new code should join on**, and the one the who-worked signal and the clock-feed matcher use (`Martínez, LESLIEE` == `LESLIEE Martinez`) |
| `loosely_same_person` | a shared first token, a substring | a generous **screening** rule — proven non-transitive in the lock (`Amir Khan` ~ `Amir` ~ `Amir Hassan`), so never a grouping key |

Plus the presentation fact collapsing two spellings immediately raises — *which one do we show?*
`best_spelling` / `collapse`: the **roster's** spelling wins (what an administrator typed), else a
comma-free form beats `Last, First`, else more words beat fewer, else alphabetical — so the chosen
name never depends on which feed loaded first.

**It is deliberately not fuzzy.** `Abdul K` and `Abdul Kakar` — both live house punch spellings —
stay two people. Merging them is a judgement a human makes; a key that made it silently would
sometimes merge two real people, which is the costlier error.

**The who-worked signal now unions PEOPLE.** `_who_worked_by_store` collapses both signals on
`folded_token_key`, reads `storeops.employees` for the authoritative spelling, and buckets **both**
signals on `account/store_identity.store_key` (§64) — previously the sales row resolved its store and
the punch's `store_code` went in raw, so a punch stamped `b-418` bucketed apart from `B-418` and its
rep vanished from the real store's day.

**And "who worked" is no longer the same field as "who was expected".** `_who_worked_display_by_store`
returns `worked` (actual only) and `scheduled` (the roster guess, only when nothing actual exists) as
**two fields**. A caller reading `worked` *cannot* print a guess as a fact. All three screens render
them apart, and §48.8 exports the guess under a heading that says what it is — `Scheduled (nobody
worked)`.

### CORE-08.4 PROOF

- `backend/harness_person_identity.py` — **95 passed / 0 failed**. §A is byte-identity: replicas of
  all five moved rules as they stood on `main` are the oracle over a 47-name corpus of the live
  spellings, so the move is proven not to have changed any caller's answer. §A2 pins the two modules
  that each claimed the question. §B reproduces the owner's cell. §D the non-fuzzy guarantees. §E the
  non-transitivity that justifies the fourth function. §F the lock: nine dereferences each one line,
  no seventh copy of the comma reorder or the first-token fallback anywhere, the home's import-time
  purity, and every screen rendering the guess apart. §G six controls.
- `backend/harness_cash_pickup_who_worked.py` — **35 passed / 0 failed**, extended with §9, which
  drives the **real** classifier over the in-memory client on the owner's own fixture: one punch, one
  sale, two spellings, **one** entry, tagged `clocked+sold`, with both raw spellings kept for the
  recon and the lower-case store code folded onto the right store-day. Its §3 assertions were
  UPDATED, not dropped — the flattened `worked` list was the defect.

Both run in CI (`carrier-vocab-guard`; the who-worked proof in the installed-dependencies job,
because it imports the closing router). `harness_cash_pickup_who_worked.py` came OFF
`harness_unrun_pending.txt` — the debt list shrank by one, 322 → 321.

### CORE-08.5 WHAT IT REGISTERS

**No table, no migration, no endpoint, no report.** `GET /closing/accountability-chain` and
`GET /closing/pickups` each gain one FIELD (`scheduled_only`) on an answer they already gave, so §16
(by TABLE) and §17 (by ENDPOINT) carry no new row and §18 (by METRIC) nothing new to measure — the
numbers did not change, which people they name did. The duplicate check (CLAUDE.md build gate) is
this section's own §CORE-08.2 table: nine existing mechanisms found, **nine extended or
dereferenced, none siblinged** — and the one new file exists precisely so there is one fewer rule in
the building, not one more. Registered in `core/module_graph.FACTS['person_identity']`.


## §CORE-09. A CAPABILITY WITHOUT A DOOR IS NOT A FEATURE — one card, three surfaces (owner 2026-10-14)

Owner: *"provide a link to reset the password for the employee log in on payroll Dash board make a
tile called Manage employee and move emplpouyee and pay and employe database along with password
reset under that tile - in both config and this new link to password reset, teh admin should be able
to assign a manual password aalso"*.

### CORE-09.1 Two of the three asks were already built

Read carefully, the request is three things, and only one of them was missing code:

| ask | state before this ship |
|---|---|
| assign a MANUAL (typed) password to an employee login | **already built, already correct** |
| a password-reset door on the Payroll dashboard | missing |
| that door, and "config", both able to assign a manual password | the capability existed; the DOORS did not |

`POST /api/v1/core/users/set-password` (`core/router.py::admin_set_password`) has always set a
SPECIFIC admin-chosen password: `validate_password` against the tenant policy server-side, a
`require_change` toggle writing `app_users.must_reset_password`, an audit row through
`_audit_auth_event("password_admin_set", …)`, and a gate on `_can_edit_setting(caller, "security")`
— a per-role grant at `permissions.settings.security`, which a full-scope admin holds by default. Its
own docstring already said it *"generalizes create-login / Reset pw — one path, not a fork"*. An
email that already signs in to another tenant cannot have a password set for it (consent), and gets
the same uniform invite response, so the endpoint is not an enumeration oracle either.

So nothing about the capability was wrong. What was wrong is that its only UI was the last card on
**Admin → Security Settings**, a page tagged `module: 'admin'` in `rbac.ts` — which an HR manager, a
district manager or anyone else who actually manages employees never sees. **A capability with no
door for the people who need it is not a feature**, and the owner found that out by looking for it.

Meanwhile `Admin → Roles & Access` → **👥 Assign people** — the screen where logins are made — offered
`⚡ Provision all assigned`, `📧 Resend` and `🔎 reveal-code`, every one of which issues a **GENERATED**
code. There was no way to type a password on the screen whose whole job is logins. That is the "in
config" half of the ask.

### CORE-09.2 THE CLASS, not the instance

The instance is *"the Payroll hub has no password link"*. The class is **a capability reachable from
exactly one surface, when three surfaces need it** — and the patchwork answer to that is to retype
the form on each new surface. Three copies of one question: the picker, the `fetch`, and the client
echo of the password policy, each free to drift from the server's `validate_password` the next time
the policy gains a rule. That is the duplicate defect the index rules already forbid.

### CORE-09.3 THE FIX — one card, dereferenced, and it cannot un-wire

**`frontend/src/components/AssignPasswordCard.tsx`** IS "assign a password to an employee login", for
every surface that offers it. It holds the one `POST /core/users/set-password` call in the frontend,
the one `pwErrors` policy echo, the picker, the require-change toggle, and — this is the important
part — it reads `can_edit` from `GET /core/security-settings` and **says in words** that the viewer
lacks the Security grant rather than rendering a form that 403s. Three surfaces render it and none
holds a copy:

| surface | why it is there |
|---|---|
| `/admin/security` | where the card used to be written out inline |
| `/admin/roles` → 👥 Assign people | **"in config"** — the screen where logins are provisioned, resent and revealed |
| `/hr/employee-password` | the Payroll hub's **Manage Employees** tile, the owner's new door — **and, since 2026-10-19, its own `Payroll & HR` side-menu row as well (§CORE-09.6)** |

**THE SERVER STAYS THE AUTHORITY.** `can_edit` only decides whether to SHOW the form.
`admin_set_password` gates independently on `_can_edit_setting(caller, "security")` and re-validates
the password, so putting the card on an `hr`-module page widens **nobody's** access: an HR manager
without the grant is told so, and a forged POST is refused 403. Same precedent as
`rbac.ts::MGMT_ONLY` — a page whose NAV tier mirrors a server gate.

**THE DESIGN CALL: a new `hr` route, not a link to `/admin/security`.** A tile needs a destination,
and the cheap destination was the page that already had the card. It does not work, and the reason is
§CORE-06: a tile is a menu entry, so `hub-gate.ts::canOpen` asks whether the viewer may open it, and
`/admin/security` is `module: 'admin'`. Measured through the shipped gate against the real role rows,
the owner's new tile would have shown the password door to **a full admin and nobody else** — not to
Cellfonz HR, not to a district manager. The proof runs that rejected design on purpose so nobody
"simplifies" it back. The new route is `module: 'hr'`, `scopes: ['all','market']` and SHIPPED `tileOnly: true` —
the shape of the two tiles it was folded beside — and renders the SAME component.

### CORE-09.4 THE TILE

The Payroll hub (`/payroll`) had `Employees & Pay` and `Employee Database` as two adjacent
single-link tiles. They are now the first two items of **👥 Manage Employees**, joined by
**🔑 Employee Password Reset**:

| door | page |
|---|---|
| Employees & Pay | `/hr?tab=employees` (where pay is SET, §19.40) |
| Employee Database | `/hr/employee-database` (read-only, exportable, carries no pay column) |
| Employee Password Reset | `/hr/employee-password` (new; **also a side-menu row since 2026-10-19 — §CORE-09.6**) |

**§19.40 IS UNTOUCHED.** That ruling (owner 2026-10-02) was about the SIDE MENU: NAV still carries
`Employees & Pay → /hr?tab=employees` as its own, non-`tileOnly` row, and the lock still pins it. This
changed only which tile the hub groups its door under — which is what the owner asked for.
`harness_nav_deep_link_lock.py` **C10** was re-expressed rather than deleted: it used to assert a tile
TITLED "Employees & Pay", which was one implementation of the ruling; it now asserts the hub carries a
door *labelled* "Employees & Pay" pointing at the tab, whichever tile groups it, plus a control (C10b)
that goes red if the label leaves.

### CORE-09.5 PROOF

- `backend/harness_assign_password_one_home.py` — **48 passed / 0 failed** (47 as shipped 2026-10-14; §CORE-09.6 re-expressed D7 and added the Z10 control), and **armed**: on pristine
  `origin/main` it reports **29 failed**, so it is a lock and not a description. Static on purpose —
  every failure mode here is a missing or duplicated wire: a surface that re-implements the card
  compiles and looks right, a surface that drops it simply shows nothing, and a tile that loses a door
  is still a valid tile. §A the one home carries the whole affordance; §B all three surfaces render it;
  §C nobody holds a second copy (not the endpoint call, not the policy echo, not a second `pwErrors`);
  §D the tile holds the owner's three doors and the two folded-in tiles are gone; §E the server gate,
  the server-side policy check and the audit row are intact and the new page carries no client-side
  role guess; §Z eleven armed controls.
- `frontend/scratchpad/prove_manage_employees_tile.mjs` — **28 passed / 0 failed** (24 as shipped 2026-10-14; §CORE-09.6 re-expressed §5) (**8 failed** on
  pristine `origin/main`). A verbatim re-impl of the shipped `rbac.ts` / `hub-gate.ts` predicates run
  against the REAL NAV parsed out of `rbac.ts`, the REAL tile literal parsed out of the hub, and the
  REAL production role rows. §2 is the load-bearing one: the rejected `/admin/security` design is shown
  dropping the password door for Cellfonz HR and the district manager while the shipped design opens
  all three doors for both; §4 a store- or self-scoped rep gets the whole tile dropped rather than a
  tile of dead links.
- CI: org-scope-guard job **Assign-password one home** runs both.
- **Two neighbouring ratchets moved, both downward.** A new page must be FINDABLE: `/hr/employee-password`
  is registered in `frontend/src/lib/route-index.ts` with the words somebody looking for it actually types
  ("reset an employee password", "assign a password", "manual password"), which is the §54.7 lesson from
  `/account/password` — the page a search for "password reset" used to miss entirely. Its entry carries NO
  `label`, because the page's wording belongs to NAV and a second spelling is the duplicate that registry's
  own §G forbids; it was added by hand rather than by `--bless`, which re-sorts entries `main` has out of
  order and drops the in-file notes. And the lint register SHRANK: moving the card out of `/admin/security`
  took two `any` annotations with it, so `eslint_pending.txt` reads 14 for that page instead of 16 and
  `harness_frontend_lint_lock.PINNED_TOTAL` drops 5645 → 5643 (§CORE-02).

**No migration, and no money moves.** No table, column or endpoint was added — `app_users`,
`must_reset_password` and `set-password` all pre-date this. Nothing here reads or writes pay.

Same class: §CORE-06 (a tile that did not ask the menu's question), §19.18 (a mechanism written and
its callers left unwired), §19.40 (the owner could not find the screen that already existed).


### CORE-09.6 A SECOND DOOR, NOT A MOVED ONE — the owner reverses `tileOnly` for this one page (owner 2026-10-19)

Owner, verbatim: *"dont drop it from anywhere jsut add a seaprate link under eh manage employee tile
under Payroll & HR"* — answering his own 2026-10-17 *"just make it a link under the manage employee
tile"*, after being asked whether he meant dropping the `Employees & Pay` side-menu row.

**The answer read as an instruction: remove NOTHING, ADD one link.** `/hr/employee-password`
("Employee Password Reset") now has its own visible row in the side menu's **Payroll & HR** group,
beside the `Employees & Pay` row. The Manage Employees tile keeps **all three** doors, `Employees & Pay`
keeps its §19.40 row, and `Employee Database` stays `tileOnly` — he named one link, not two.

**This is a deliberate owner reversal of the W2.1 "cleaner look" ruling, for this one page.** W2.1 made
every non-hub item in `Payroll & HR` `tileOnly` so the group's sidebar would be short, and §CORE-09.3
shipped the password page inside that ruling. The ruling is not repealed — one page is exempted from it
on the owner's word, which is now written on the NAV entry itself so the next tidy-up reads the reason
before deleting the row.

**NOBODY'S ACCESS CHANGED, and the server is still the only authority.** The row carries the same
`module: 'hr'`, `scopes: ['all','market']` it had as a tile door, and `rbac.ts::canSeeItem` already
gated the item in both renderings — `tileOnly` is a *sidebar render-skip*, never a gate (W2.1
precedent). Actually setting a password is still `POST /core/users/set-password` gated on
`_can_edit_setting(caller, "security")`, so an HR manager without that grant sees the row, opens the
page and is told in words that they lack the Security grant.

| | before (2026-10-14) | after (2026-10-19) |
|---|---|---|
| Manage Employees tile doors | 3 | 3 — unchanged |
| `Payroll & HR` visible rows | `Payroll Dashboard`, `Employees & Pay` | `Payroll Dashboard`, `Employees & Pay`, **`Employee Password Reset`** |
| NAV entry `tileOnly` | `true` | *absent* |
| module / scopes / server gate | `hr` / `['all','market']` / `security` | unchanged |

**THE LOCKS WERE RE-EXPRESSED, NOT RELAXED.** Both pins that encoded `tileOnly` now pin the NEW shape
and are armed against the old one returning, so the row cannot be tidied away silently:

- `backend/harness_assign_password_one_home.py` **D7** flipped from *"…and tileOnly, because the tile IS
  its door"* to *"…and NOT tileOnly: it carries its own side-menu row"*, and **tightened**: with **D2**
  still pinning the tile's three doors, the page must now have BOTH doors rather than either. New
  armed control **Z10** goes red if `tileOnly: true` is restored on the row. **48 passed / 0 failed.**
- `frontend/scratchpad/prove_manage_employees_tile.mjs` **§5** asserts the parsed row is non-`tileOnly`,
  that the tile door is still there, and that the group's visible rows are exactly
  `/payroll`, `/hr?tab=employees`, `/hr/employee-password` — with its own control for `tileOnly`
  restored. **28 passed / 0 failed.**
- Re-run unchanged and green: `harness_nav_deep_link_lock.py` (60, C10/C10b untouched — they pin the
  HUB door's label, not the sidebar), `harness_hub_viewer_gate.py` (53),
  `harness_roles_module_catalog.py` (34), `prove_tile_hubs.mjs` (118 — `Payroll & HR` is in its
  `skip` list, so its "every other item in a converted group is `tileOnly`" rule never applied here),
  `prove_nav_layout.mjs` (20).

**Duplicate check.** No new route, component, endpoint, table or report — one existing NAV entry lost
one flag. The sidebar row and the tile door are two renderings of the SAME `rbac.ts` NAV item through
the SAME `canSeeItem` predicate, which is the no-second-path shape, not a violation of it. No
migration, no money path.


## §CORE-10. A GATE, NOT A NOTE — the branch's base, and a guard that goes blind (owner 2026-10-14)

Owner, on being told about two near-misses that had been caught by hand and written down:
*"this is very creitical finding , dont jsut write down make a gate so nothing can passs thru
unkowlingly , you were smart may be the other might not be as asmart"*.

That is the whole ruling, and it generalises past these two bugs: **a lesson that lives in a note is
enforced by whoever happens to remember it. A lesson that lives in CI is enforced.** Both failures
below were silent — neither produced a red tick, and both were found by someone counting things by
hand on a day they happened to be suspicious.

### CORE-10.1 THE TWO FAILURES, and the one fact they share

| | What happened | Why nothing went red |
|---|---|---|
| **The stale base** (PR #475, 2026-10-14) | `git checkout -b <branch>` was run with no start point, so the branch was cut from the session's already-merged branch instead of `origin/main`. The pull request carried 5 already-squash-merged commits and its two-dot diff against `main` **deleted 103,263 lines over 498 files**. | The conflict it created means GitHub starts **no `pull_request` workflow at all** (see §19 on `mergeable_state: dirty`), so the only green tick came from the preview deployment, which proves nothing about the guards. |
| **The guard that went blind** (PR #477, 2026-10-14) | `harness_browser_sweep_kinds.py` DERIVES the endpoints that can reach a live browser by scanning `supply/router.py`, then asserts each one calls `require_browser_service()` — the `core/service_role.py` gate that keeps a
`SERVICE_ROLE=api` deploy from faking a browser session. Moving that call into a helper made `read_vendor_catalog` leave the derived set — so its guard assertion **did not fail, it stopped existing**. | The only assertion about the set itself was `len(reach) >= 4`. It went red because the bound sat exactly at four. One more endpoint in the set and the hole ships green. |

The shared fact: **a check decided for itself what it was checking.** One decided which tree it was
proving; the other decided which subjects it was guarding. Where that judgement is implicit, it is
also silent, so it is made explicit here and failed in CI when it is wrong.

### CORE-10.2 GATE A — the branch was cut from its base

`scripts/check_branch_base.py`, three failures, every one of them a symptom a human has to be looking
for today:

- **A2 mass deletion.** The TWO-DOT diff `base..head` removes more than 2,000 lines. A genuinely large
  removal is still allowed — it must SAY SO, by carrying `BASE-DELETIONS-ACKNOWLEDGED` in the pull
  request body, which puts the declaration where a reviewer reads it. Silence is the failure.
- **A3 re-proposed merged work.** A commit on the branch whose SUBJECT already exists in the base
  branch's history. Subjects, because this repo squash-merges: a merged commit is not an ancestor of
  `main`, so ancestry cannot answer the question and `git diff main...branch` (three dots) actively
  lies — its merge base lands before the squash, and merged content renders as new. Two agents were
  misled by exactly that on 2026-09-29 (CLAUDE.md records it).
- **A4 a lost CI job.** Any job name declared on the base branch and absent from the head branch's
  workflow files, named. This is the 2026-10-10 trap on PR #440: a `pull_request` run executes the
  workflow file **from the head branch**, so a branch cut before `main` added a job never runs that
  job, forever, however often CI is re-run. 48 green checks next to main's 51 read as finished.

### CORE-10.3 WHY GATE A RUNS ON `pull_request_target`, and the rule that comes with it

A gate that lives in the branch's own workflow file is precisely what a stale branch drops — failure
A4 would delete this guard itself. `.github/workflows/branch-base-guard.yml` is therefore triggered
from the BASE branch, which is the only trigger here that is.

**The safety rule, stated so nobody relaxes it:** that job never checks out and never executes code
from the pull request. It fetches the head as git data, reads commit subjects, and parses workflow
TEXT. It holds `permissions: contents: read`, `persist-credentials: false` and no secrets, and the PR
body reaches the script through a file written from an env var, never interpolated into a shell
command. Do not add a step to it that runs a script, an install or a build from the PR's tree.

### CORE-10.4 GATE B — a guard may not quietly decide what it is still guarding

`backend/harness_subject_set_lock.py`. **A guard whose subjects are derived from the code must compare
them with a DECLARED set, both ways — not assert a lower bound on how many it found.** A lower bound
tolerates substitution (one subject in, one out), tolerates the scan's own axis going blind, and never
names what left. The right shape was already in the offending file, ten lines above the wrong one:
`eq(derived, BROWSER_MODULES_ELSEWHERE, …)`.

So `harness_browser_sweep_kinds.py` now declares `SUPPLY_BROWSER_ENDPOINTS` and compares the derived
set to it. Proof that this is a tighter lock and not a restatement: renaming the browser call in one
endpoint used to lower a count, and now reports *"got {open_order_session, submit_order,
capture_confirmation} want {…, read_vendor_catalog}"* — it names the endpoint that left.

**A ratchet, not a sweep.** 51 sites were measured across 41 harnesses on 2026-10-14; most are
harmless fixture sanity, and rewriting all of them in one change is a diff nobody can review. The 50
that remain are pinned in `backend/harness_subject_set_pending.txt` with their own assertion label as
the reason, **a NEW site fails the build**, a stale pin fails the build (it would re-permit the weak
form silently), and `PINNED_MAX` means the list may only shrink. Same shape as
`harness_unrun_pending.txt` and `frontend/table_sort_pending.txt`.

Gate B is the sibling of the pipefail lock and sits beside it in `security.yml` for that reason: that
one fails a build when a guard goes **red** unnoticed, this one when a guard goes **blind** unnoticed.

### CORE-10.5 WHAT WAS REUSED, NOT REBUILT (duplicate check — build gate)

Searched the index and the harness tree for anything already answering "was this branch cut from a
current base" and "is this guard still guarding its subjects". Nothing was: the branch-lifecycle rules
in CLAUDE.md and the memory notes on both traps are **prose**, which is what the owner's ruling is
about. What already existed and is dereferenced rather than copied:

- `harness_ci_pipefail_lock.py` stays the ONE home for "a workflow that runs a gate declares
  `defaults: run: shell: bash`". Its axis was **widened** from `harness_*.py` to gate scripts
  (`scripts/check_*.py`) rather than given a second copy of the rule — the branch-base guard is the
  first gate to live outside `backend/`, and the lock could not see it. `deploy-reachability.yml`
  gained the default in the same change, since the widened axis covers it.
- The debt-list idiom (a pinned, shrink-only list plus `PINNED_MAX`) is reused verbatim from that same
  lock, not reinvented.
- `harness_browser_sweep_kinds.py` keeps its own `eq()` / `_effective_body()`; Gate B holds no copy of
  the browser rule, only the rule about the SHAPE of such a check.

### CORE-10.6 LOCKED SO IT CANNOT UN-WIRE, and armed

- **Gate A**: 10 negative controls, run in CI as its own step (`--self-test`). The planted defects are
  the real shapes — a job deleted from the head's workflow file, a re-proposed squash subject, a file
  the base added and the branch removed — built in a throwaway git repository, so they cannot rot.
  Verified against the live remote: a real merged `claude/*` branch fails A2 (207,236 lines) and A4
  (53 jobs named), and this branch passes all three.
- **Gate B**: 7 negative controls, including two the first draft would have failed. The detector masks
  string literals and comments before reading paren depth, because unmasked it found 35 of the 51 real
  sites and would have pinned a short list and then silently passed what it could not see — the same
  class of defect it exists to catch. `Z5` proves the weak form written in prose is not a site, `Z4`
  that a site wrapped over four lines past a stray paren still is.
- Neither bound was relaxed to go green. `PINNED_MAX` is 50 and may only fall.

### CORE-10.7 WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, STATED

- A2 reads a THRESHOLD. A branch cut from a base two days old deletes nothing and passes, correctly —
  what it can still lose is a CI job, which is A4's job to name.
- A3 compares subjects, so a branch that rewrites a merged commit's message re-proposes it undetected.
  A4 and A2 both still fire on that shape, and the structural fix for branch reuse is GitHub's
  **Settings → General → "Automatically delete head branches"**, which is owner-only and still off.
- Gate B reads a SHAPE, not a meaning: it cannot tell a fixture's size from a list of code sites. That
  is why each pinned row carries its own assertion label — the reader tells them apart, and the
  dangerous ones are the rows whose set is a list of code sites.
- The 50 pinned sites are not fixed. They are declared, bounded and shrink-only.

Same class: §19.25 (a failing harness that did not fail CI), §19.28 and the `vacuous-check-trap`
instances (a check that cannot fail), §13a (a scanner blind to a second syntactic form), §19.18 (a
mechanism written and its callers left unwired).

## §CORE-11. A COLUMN THAT DRAWS ITS OWN CELL IS DRAWN — one body-cell home per table (owner report 2026-10-15)

Owner, on the two seller-declared cells shipped the day before (§COMMCALC-03.26): *"it did not let
is enter"*. There was nothing to type into. The box had never been on the screen.

### CORE-11.1 THE CLASS — one question, two answers, one of them silently wrong

`lib/export.tsx` declares `ExportColumn.render` — *"custom cell rendering"* — and it is how an
interactive cell (a button, a picker, a box you type in) reaches the screen at all. Two components
take that column definition:

| | body cell | result |
|---|---|---|
| `components/DataGrid.tsx` | `c.render ? c.render(r) : defaultCell(c, r)` | honoured the contract |
| `components/ReportShell.tsx` | `isMoney(c) ? money(c.get(r)) : str(c.get(r))`, in **two** row paths | ignored it |

Nothing failed while that was true, which is why it lasted: the column was accepted, its callback
was simply never called, and the page rendered the plain value where its author had put a control.
**Three shipped columns were dead that way, all on `commcalc/store-takeover`:**

- the evaluations list's **Open** button — with the page copy directly above it reading *"Press Open
  on any row"*. The Prospect dropdown was the only way into an evaluation, which is how the hole
  stayed invisible.
- its **Compare with our store** picker (§COMMCALC-03.25, shipped 2026-10-14).
- the two **seller-declared cells** (§COMMCALC-03.26, shipped 2026-10-14) — the one the owner hit.

A fourth site was found by the same question and fixed in the same change: `crm/reports/page.tsx`
renders its own bespoke table over the shared column type and dropped `render` too. It declared no
renderer today, so no user had lost anything there yet — which is exactly the shape that goes wrong
later, so it was wired rather than noted.

### CORE-11.2 THE FIX — one home, both row paths on it

`ReportShell` now holds ONE answer to "what does a body cell show":

```ts
const bodyCell = (c: Col, r: any) => (c.render ? c.render(r) : (isMoney(c) ? money(c.get(r)) : str(c.get(r))))
```

dereferenced by the plain-row path and the grouped-row path. The two inline copies are gone. All
three takeover columns light up from that one change, because the defect was never in any of them.

`render` stays **display only**. Sorting, filtering, grouping, subtotals, the total row and every
export read `get`, so a downloaded file carries the figure the control was bound to rather than a
control nobody can open. `lib/export.tsx`, which builds the PDF and Print HTML, must therefore NOT
honour `render` — it is the one excused member of the subject set below, and the lock asserts the
opposite rule on it rather than skipping it.

### CORE-11.3 LOCKED SO IT CANNOT UN-WIRE

`backend/harness_column_render_lock.py` — 32 checks, DB-free, stdlib only, wired into
`carrier-vocab-guard.yml` (its own step plus `ReportShell.tsx` / `DataGrid.tsx` / `export.tsx` in the
paths filter).

- **(a)** every table component in scope honours `render`. The subject set is **derived**: a file is
  in scope because it draws a `<td` whose content it reads off a handed column (`c.get(`), never
  because it is named — and the derived set is then held against a **named roster** of three, each
  member with its reason, so a member that leaves says so instead of quietly losing its assertion
  (§CORE-10's gate B; a bare `len(...) >= 2` was the first draft here and that lock caught it). It
  deliberately does not catch a page
  that hand-writes `<td>{r.day}</td>` per field while keeping an `ExportColumn` list for its export
  (`closing/accountability`): that page reads no column accessor, so it has nothing to drop.
- **(b)** exactly ONE `bodyCell` home in `ReportShell` and exactly two dereferences of it; the inline
  `isMoney(c) ? money(c.get(r))` body cell — the copy that caused this — fails the build.
- **(c)** `render` stays display-only: `lib/export.tsx` declares it and never calls it.
- **(d)** every page declaring a renderer hands it to a component that honours one.
- **(e)** negative controls plant each defect, including the excused member and the out-of-scope page
  shape, and require the lock to catch or spare them correctly.
- **(regression)** the three columns that were blank are asserted present by name.

### CORE-11.4 WHY NOT A TYPE

`render?:` is optional by design — most columns want none — so no compiler can tell "this component
may be handed a column with a renderer" from "this component honours one". The distinction is
behavioural, which is why it needs a behavioural check. Same reasoning as §CORE-10's gate B.

Same class: §19.18 (a mechanism written and its callers left unwired — this is its fourth instance),
§19.29 (218 tables that never reached the sorting mechanism that already existed), §CORE-10 (a lesson
in a note is enforced by whoever remembers it).
